claims.text: Replacing 20% of the Hf sublattice with Al produces the nominal composition (Hf0.8Al0.2)MoTaTiZr.
Partial replacement of Hf by Al will reduce the alloy density.
Al lowers density because it is lighter than Hf and lowers the alloy's average atomic mass.
The modified alloy will retain a single-phase BCC solid solution.
Al addition may form fine, coherent precipitates in the BCC matrix.
Atomic-size mismatch can promote solid-solution strengthening in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The Al-for-Hf substitution creates sufficient atomic-size mismatch and suitable mixing enthalpy to robustly strengthen (Hf0.8Al0.2)MoTaTiZr.
Fine, coherent Al-related precipitates would hinder dislocation motion and provide precipitation strengthening.
The modified alloy will maintain or slightly improve yield strength and ductility at room temperature.
The modified alloy will maintain or slightly improve yield strength and ductility at approximately 1000 °C.
The expected density reduction is approximately 10–20% relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm3.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr exhibits high strength and ductility at room and elevated temperatures.
Validation is restricted to quasi-static tensile and compressive loading at room temperature and approximately 1000 °C.
Retention of a single-phase BCC structure is critical to successful mechanical performance.
A density reduction below 10% would falsify the hypothesis.
A loss of more than 10% in yield strength or ductility at either test temperature would falsify the hypothesis.
Formation of harmful secondary phases that compromise the desired microstructure would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and boundary require a single-phase BCC alloy, while the structural mediator and mechanism also invoke Al-induced precipitates. Distinct precipitates would ordinarily make the microstructure multiphase unless they are merely coherent compositional clusters within the same BCC phase.
